## Introduction — Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs)

- NETs are a **heterogeneous group of neoplasms** originating from the diffuse neuroendocrine cell system
- Most commonly arise in the **lung** or **gastrointestinal (GI) tract**
- Although a rarer group of neoplasms:
  - NET **incidence and prevalence continue to increase**
  - NETs are now the **second most prevalent GI cancer**

## Introduction — Defining PNETs

- Well-differentiated NETs are subdivided largely by **tissue of origin**
- **Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs)** arise from the endocrine tissue of the pancreas — the **islets of Langerhans**
- PNETs are the **second most common tumor** arising from the pancreas

## Introduction — Making a Comprehensive Diagnosis

- A comprehensive PNET diagnosis relies on evaluation of:
  - **Clinical symptoms**
  - **Imaging**
  - **Histopathology**

## Introduction — Why Management Is Challenging

- Management and treatment of PNETs is challenging because of:
  - **Heterogeneity in tumor behavior**
  - **Heterogeneity in clinical presentation**
- Approximately **30% of PNETs are functional** — producing clinical symptoms from hormone hypersecretion

## Introduction — Observation First, Then Treatment

- Many advanced PNETs can be **monitored initially** because of **indolent growth patterns**
- With time, the disease will require treatment
- Decision to start therapy is triggered by:
  - Increasing clinical symptoms (hormone secretion and/or tumor bulk)
  - High tumor burden
  - Progressive disease while on observation

## Introduction — Treatment Landscape

- Treatment options for PNETs are **multidisciplinary**:
  - Surgical resection
  - Liver-directed therapies
  - Systemic treatments
- For metastatic PNETs, treatment is **almost always noncurative**
- Survival can often be measured **in years**, but **most patients die of the disease**

## Epidemiology — Key Statistics

- PNETs account for approximately:
  - **7% of all NETs**
  - **1% to 2% of pancreatic tumors**

## Epidemiology — Rising Incidence

- Incidence has risen over the past **30 years**:
  - From **0.17** to **0.43 cases per 100,000 people**

## Epidemiology — Who Gets PNETs?

- **Males and females are affected equally**
- Most patients are diagnosed between **60 and 80 years** of age
- Approximately **5%** of patients have an underlying familial syndrome:
  - MEN1, VHL, tuberous sclerosis (TS), or NF1
  - These patients tend to be diagnosed at a **younger age**

## Epidemiology — Risk Factors

- A **family history of NET** is the **only well-established risk factor** for PNET development
- Risk factors for pancreatic adenocarcinoma have **NOT** been associated with PNETs:
  - Cigarette smoking
  - Diabetes mellitus
  - Chronic pancreatitis
  - Obesity

## Molecular Biology — First Sequencing Efforts

- In one of the earliest studies:
  - **Whole-exome sequencing (WES)** performed on **10 nonfamilial PNETs**
  - Most commonly mutated genes screened in an additional **58 PNET specimens**

## Molecular Biology — Whole-Exome Findings

- Increased number of mutations identified in:
  - **Chromatin remodeling genes:** MEN1, DAXX, ATRX
  - **mTOR pathway genes:** PTEN, TSC2, PIK3CA
- These pathways became foundational to understanding sporadic PNET biology

## Molecular Biology — Whole-Genome Sequencing

- Whole-genome sequencing performed on **102 PNETs**
- Somatic point mutations and gene fusions observed in **four pathways**:
  - Chromatin remodeling
  - DNA damage repair
  - mTOR
  - **Telomere maintenance**
- A larger-than-anticipated **germline contribution** was identified:
  - Previously unreported germline mutations in DNA repair genes **MUTYH, CHEK2, BRCA2**

## Molecular Biology — NGS in the Clinic

- Next-generation sequencing (NGS) assessed in **96 tumor samples from 80 patients** with metastatic PNETs
- **Somatic alterations identified in 95%** of tested tumor samples
- Most commonly altered genes: **MEN1, DAXX, ATRX, TSC2**
- Sequencing of pre- and post-treatment samples revealed:
  - **Progression in tumor grade**
  - **Clonal evolution** of tumors

## Molecular Biology — Germline Findings in Metastatic PNET

- Germline analysis identified alterations in **high-penetrance autosomal dominant cancer susceptibility genes**:
  - MEN1
  - TSC2
  - VHL
- Supports a role for genetic testing in the routine clinic setting

## Molecular Biology — PNECs Are Distinct

- Poorly differentiated **pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinomas (PNECs)** are **clinically and genetically distinct** from PNETs
- Most commonly mutated genes in PNECs (tumor suppressors):
  - **p53 — 95%**
  - **Rb — 74%**

## Pathology — Gross Features

- PNETs are generally:
  - **Well-circumscribed**
  - **Solitary masses**
  - Can occur **anywhere in the pancreas**
- The **majority of PNETs are well differentiated**

## Pathology — All PNETs Have Malignant Potential

- All PNETs have the potential to **grow and eventually metastasize**
- Because of this, these tumors are **considered malignant**
- The term **"benign"** has been used as a classification variable only because metastatic likelihood is **very low** in certain subsets

## Pathology — Features Defining Malignancy

Most classification schemes consider a PNET **malignant** if it:

- Invades locoregionally
- Has metastasized distantly or to regional lymph nodes
- Is **> 2 cm** in size
- Displays **vascular, lymphatic, or perineural invasion**
- Has a **proliferative index > 2%**

## Pathology — WHO 2017 Classification

- PNETs are classified by the **2017 WHO classification of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs)**
- Pathologic classification by WHO 2017 is the **most significant prognostic tool**:
  - Predicts tumor behavior
  - Guides treatment selection
- Stratification is by:
  - **Differentiation:** well or poorly differentiated
  - **Grade:** G1 (low), G2 (intermediate), G3 (high) — by Ki-67 and/or mitotic count

## TABLE 65.1 — Grading System for Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors

| Terminology | Differentiation | Grade | Mitotic rate (mitoses/2 mm²) | Ki-67 index (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NET, G1 | Well differentiated | Low | <2 | <3 |
| NET, G2 | Well differentiated | Intermediate | 2 to 20 | 3 to 20 |
| NET, G3 | Well differentiated | High | >20 | >20 |
| NEC (small cell or non-small cell) | Poorly differentiated | High | >20 | >20 |

*From: Lloyd RV, Osamura RY, Klöppel G, et al. WHO Classification of Tumours of Endocrine Organs. IARC; 2017.*

## TABLE 65.1 — Notes on the Grading System

- Poorly differentiated NECs are **not formally graded** but are considered **high grade by definition**
- This system is recommended by the **European Neuroendocrine Tumor Society (ENETS)** and the **World Health Organization**
- It is the **most widely used grading system** and the method used by most surgical pathology laboratories

## Pathology — Measuring Mitoses and Ki-67

- **Mitotic index:** number of mitotic figures per 10 high-powered microscopic fields (HPFs)
  - Recommended that **40 to 50 HPFs** be examined
- **Ki-67 labeling:**
  - Tags neoplastic cells with an antibody
  - Reports the **percentage of cells that stain positively**

## Pathology — Terminology: NET vs NEC

- **Well-differentiated** NENs are defined as **tumors (NETs)**
- **Poorly differentiated** NENs are defined as **carcinomas (NECs)**
- The 2017 classification recognizes **heterogeneity of grade 3** pancreatic NENs:
  - Well-differentiated **NET G3** vs. poorly differentiated **NEC** — distinct subtypes

## Pathology — Why the WHO Classification Evolved

- Changes from WHO 2010 to 2017 evolved through understanding of:
  - **Distinct treatment responses** for grade 3 PNETs vs. PNECs
  - **Distinct clinical outcomes** for grade 3 PNETs vs. PNECs

## Staging — AJCC TNM (2017)

- Most commonly used staging system in the United States: **2017 American Joint Committee on Cancer tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) system**
- **Stage I** — localized tumors
- **Stages II and III** — more advanced local or regional disease
- **Stage IV** — distant metastases

## Staging — SEER Survival by Stage

- 5-year overall survival (OS), functional and nonfunctional tumors combined (SEER database):
  - **Localized:** 62%
  - **Regionally advanced:** 54%
  - **Distant metastases:** 20%

## Prognosis — The Paradox of Well-Differentiated Tumors

- Despite being classified as well differentiated, the **majority of PNETs**:
  - Have pathologic features that increase the likelihood of **future recurrence**, **or**
  - Have **metastatic disease at the time of diagnosis**

## Prognosis — Survival by Grade

- 5-year OS by grade:
  - **G1 (low):** 75%
  - **G2 (intermediate):** 63%
  - **G3 (high):** 7%
- Low- and intermediate-grade PNETs have significantly better survival than G3 tumors

## Prognosis — Functional Status Matters

- **Functional tumors** are associated with better survival than nonfunctional PNETs:
  - **68% vs. 60% 5-year OS**
- Reason: functional tumors are more often identified at an **earlier stage** (symptomatic hormone hypersecretion)

## Prognosis — Distant Metastases at Presentation

- Approximately **60% of PNET cases have distant metastases at presentation**
- Metastatic disease is associated with **decreased survival** compared with local or locoregional disease

## Prognosis — Age at Diagnosis

- Older age at diagnosis correlates with **impaired survival**:
  - **< 55 years:** 67.8% 5-year OS
  - **> 75 years:** 40.8% 5-year OS
- Age helps stratify patients into prognostic categories

## Familial Syndromes — Overview

- PNETs are associated with **four familial diseases**:
  - **MEN1** (most common)
  - **VHL**
  - **NF1**
  - **Tuberous sclerosis (TS)**

## MEN1 — The Most Common Syndrome

- Approximately **5% to 7%** of patients with PNETs have **MEN1**
- Inherited in an **autosomal dominant** fashion

## MEN1 — Classic Manifestations

- **Parathyroid adenomas** → hyperparathyroidism in **90%** of patients
- **Multiple functional or nonfunctional PNETs** in **75%**
- **Pituitary adenomas** in **40%**

## MEN1 — Other Associated Tumors

- Also seen in some patients:
  - **Adrenocortical tumors** (functional and nonfunctional)
  - **Thymic tumors**
  - **Bronchial NETs**

## MEN1 — Genetic Testing

- Genetic testing for MEN1 should be performed in:
  - **All first-degree relatives** of affected patients (including children younger than 5 years)
  - Those who have had a **germline mutation identified in the MEN1 gene**

## MEN1 — Metastases and Mortality

- Approximately **30% to 50%** of patients present with **metastases**
- Complications of metastases are the **most common cause of death** from MEN1
- Surgical management of these tumors is **complex**

## VHL — Genetics and Tumor Spectrum

- **Autosomal dominant** syndrome caused by **inactivation of the VHL gene** (a role in angiogenesis)
- Predisposes to:
  - Renal cell carcinoma
  - Pheochromocytoma
  - Cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastoma
  - Retinal angioma
  - Endolymphatic sac neoplasms
  - Epididymal cystadenoma
  - Cystic and solid pancreatic neoplasms

## VHL — Pancreatic Disease

- **10% to 15%** of VHL patients will develop **PNETs**
- However, the most common pancreatic manifestation of VHL is **serous cystadenoma**

## Tuberous Sclerosis (TS)

- The **TSC1/2 complex inhibits mTOR**; a defect in the **TSC2 gene** leads to TS
- Hamartomas may develop in: **brain, eyes, heart, lungs, skin, kidneys, and pancreas**

## Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1)

- The **NF1 gene regulates the activity of TSC2**
- **Loss of NF1 → constitutive mTOR activation**
- Primary manifestation: **benign neurofibromas** in multiple locations of the peripheral nervous system
- Patients are also at risk for **pheochromocytomas and sarcomas**

## TS and NF1 — Pancreatic Involvement

- In **both TS and NF1**, multiple PNETs may develop in the **pancreas and duodenum**
- Shared biology: both syndromes converge on **mTOR pathway dysregulation**

## Functional Tumors — Clinical Classification

- PNETs are clinically classified into **two categories**:
  - **Functional:** produce clinical syndromes due to hypersecretion of biologically active peptides
  - **Nonfunctional:** no hormone-associated syndrome
- **~30%** of PNETs are functional

## Functional Tumors — Why They Fare Better

- Functional PNETs tend to have **better 5-year OS** than nonfunctional PNETs
- Likely because they are **detected earlier** due to the presence of symptoms

## Insulinoma — Overview

- Secrete **insulin and/or proinsulin → hypoglycemia**
- Represent **1% to 2% of all pancreatic tumors**
- Typically:
  - **Small (< 2 cm)**
  - **Solitary** (except in MEN1)
  - **Intrapancreatic**

## Insulinoma — Whipple's Triad

A critical part of the history includes establishment of **Whipple's triad**:

- Plasma glucose **< 40 mg/dL**
- **Symptoms of hypoglycemia**
- **Resolution of symptoms** with a meal

## Insulinoma — Biochemical Diagnosis

- Diagnosis confirmed by drawing during a **72-hour fast**:
  - Plasma glucose
  - Insulin
  - C-peptide
  - Proinsulin
- This panel detects **90% of insulinomas**

## Insulinoma — Malignant Behavior

- In the rare cases where insulinomas are **malignant**:
  - 5-year OS: **56%**
  - 10-year OS: **29%**
- Malignant insulinomas produce **higher levels of insulin and proinsulin** → more severe symptoms (metastases also secrete these hormones)

## Insulinoma — Localization

- Most insulinomas are identified with **CT or ultrasound (US)**
- When tumors are **very small**, these methods may fail → **arterial stimulation venous sampling (ASVS)** may be helpful

## Insulinoma — Arterial Stimulation Venous Sampling (ASVS)

- Right and left **hepatic veins catheterized** via a femoral puncture
- **Calcium injected successively** into:
  - Gastroduodenal artery
  - Proximal splenic artery
  - Superior mesenteric artery
  - Proper hepatic artery
- Venous blood sampled from hepatic veins at **30, 60, and 120 seconds** after each injection

## Insulinoma — ASVS Interpretation & Accuracy

- **Positive localization** = **2-fold increase** in hepatic vein insulin levels
- Accuracy for localizing the tumor to a pancreatic region (head, body, tail): **94% to 100%**

## Gastrinoma — Overview

- Secrete **gastrin → Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES)**
- Named for **Zollinger and colleagues (1955)**: a case series of two patients with:
  - Gastric acid hypersecretion
  - Severe peptic ulceration
  - Pancreatic tumors

## Gastrinoma — Clinical Syndrome

- Extraordinarily high gastrin levels cause:
  - **Recurrent peptic ulcers**
  - **Diarrhea**
  - **Reflux esophagitis**
- Cause the **thickened mucosal folds** in the stomach that are a hallmark of the disease

## Gastrinoma — Sporadic vs. Familial

- May be **sporadic (67%)** or **familial (33%)**
- Generally **solitary** tumors — **except in MEN1**, where they are:
  - Small
  - Multiple
  - Most likely found in the **duodenum (> 85%)**

## FIGURE 65.1 — The Gastrinoma Triangle

> **FIGURE 65.1 — Gastrinoma triangle.** Approximately **90% of gastrinomas** are thought to arise in this anatomic location. *(From Howard TJ, Stabile BE, Zinner MJ, et al. Anatomic distribution of pancreatic endocrine tumors. Am J Surg. 1990;159:258–264.)*

```
            Apex:
  cystic duct / common
      bile duct junction
              /\
             /  \
            /    \
           /      \
  Medial  /        \  Inferior
  extent  \        /  aspect
           \      /
   head–body      second–third
   junction       duodenal junction
```

## Gastrinoma Triangle — Anatomic Boundaries

- **Apex:** junction of the **cystic duct and common bile duct**
- **Inferior aspect:** junction of the **second and third parts of the duodenum**
- **Medial extent:** junction of the **head and body of the pancreas**
- Landmarks in the figure: **SMA** (superior mesenteric artery), **SMV** (superior mesenteric vein) — tumors described relative to left/right of SMA
- Described in **1984** to aid surgeons in finding these frequently **diminutive tumors**

## Gastrinoma — Malignant Behavior

- The **majority of gastrinomas are malignant (60%)**
- Have spread to **regional lymph nodes** by the time of diagnosis
- **Liver metastases** are often associated with gastrinomas arising **in the pancreas**

## Gastrinoma — Laboratory Diagnosis

- Requires demonstration of **hypergastrinemia** and **abnormal gastric acid secretion**
- Obtain:
  - **Fasting serum gastrin**
  - **Gastric pH**
- Diagnosis confirmed if: gastrin **10 times normal** AND gastric pH **< 2**

## Gastrinoma — Stimulation Tests

- If results are **equivocal**, perform a **secretin or glucagon stimulation test**
- Rationale: gastrinomas frequently **express both receptors** and respond by secreting abnormally large amounts of gastrin to the injected reagent

## Glucagonoma — Overview

- Secrete **glucagon → hyperglycemia**
- **Extremely rare** — only about **400 cases** reported in the literature
- Tend to be **large (> 6 cm)** and **solitary** pancreatic tumors

## Glucagonoma — Clinical Features

- Most common symptoms:
  - **Glucose intolerance**
  - **Migratory necrolytic erythema (MNE)** — the migratory rash is often the **first manifestation**
  - **Weight loss**
- The rash tends to start in the **perineum**, then spreads to the **trunk and extremities**

## Glucagonoma — Diagnosis & Prognosis

- Diagnosis: **elevated plasma glucagon** in the context of an **enhancing pancreatic mass on CT**
- Approximately **60% have liver metastases at diagnosis**
- In a case report of 23 glucagonomas: 5-year OS (regardless of treatment) was **nearly 75%**

## VIPoma — Overview

- Secrete **vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) → severe secretory diarrhea**
- Tend to be **solitary, intrapancreatic** tumors
- **> 50% are metastatic at presentation**

## VIPoma — Verner-Morrison Syndrome

- VIP is a **neurotransmitter and intestinal secretagogue**
- Hypersecretion causes **"pancreatic cholera"** (also known as **Verner-Morrison syndrome**):
  - **Large-volume (average 4.5 L) watery diarrhea**
  - **Metabolic acidosis**
  - **Achlorhydria**
  - **Hypokalemia**
- If not properly identified and treated → death from **renal failure secondary to hypovolemia**

## VIPoma — Diagnosis

- Diagnosis requires:
  - **Radiographic evidence** of a pancreatic tumor
  - **History consistent** with the VIP hypersecretion syndrome
  - Confirmation by **elevated plasma VIP level**

## Somatostatinoma — Overview

- **Less-defined clinical syndrome** than other functional PNETs
- Not all tumors that hypersecrete somatostatin cause symptoms
- The syndrome may include:
  - Glucose intolerance
  - Cholelithiasis
  - Weight loss
  - Diarrhea
  - Steatorrhea
  - Anemia

## Somatostatinoma — Sites & the NF1 Connection

- May arise in the **pancreas (56%)** or **duodenum**
- May be **more aggressive if intrapancreatic**
- **Duodenal somatostatinomas** are associated with **NF1 in ~50% of cases**
- If discovered in the NF1 context, they are **less likely to be malignant**

## Pancreatic Polypeptide–Secreting Tumors

- PNETs that predominantly secrete **pancreatic polypeptide (PP)** are **extremely rare**
- Whether they should be classified as **functional is debated** — no specific syndrome has been defined
- Patients may present with:
  - Intermittent abdominal pain
  - Pancreatitis
  - Glucose intolerance
- In **MEN1**, these tumors tend to be **multifocal and malignant**
- **PP as a marker in MEN1:** fasting PP levels **> 3× normal** correlate with a PNET likely large enough to detect on standard imaging

## Nonfunctional Tumors — Definition

- Characterized by **lack of hormone production** and hormone-associated syndromes
- They have the potential to produce peptides (which do **not** cause hormone-producing symptoms):
  - Pancreatic polypeptide
  - Chromogranin A
  - Ghrelin
  - Neurotensin
  - Subunits of chorionic gonadotropin
  - Neuron-specific enolase
- Patients with "nonfunctional" tumors can **develop hormone-secretion symptoms later** in their disease course

## Nonfunctional Tumors — How Common?

- The true proportion of nonfunctional PNETs is **difficult to know** — reports vary widely: **10% to 91%**

## Nonfunctional Tumors — Why Estimates Vary

- **Single-institution rates may be lower:** referral bias for functional tumors at academic medical centers
- **Large public databases (SEER, NCDB) show higher rates:**
  - Do not collect data on symptoms or hormone levels
  - Default categorization is **nonfunctional** unless a specific functional histology code is recorded (e.g., insulinoma, gastrinoma, VIPoma, glucagonoma)
- **Reasonable estimate: ~75% of PNETs are nonfunctional**

## Nonfunctional Tumors — Symptomatic Presentation

- In one report, **39%** were discovered due to **mass-effect symptoms**:
  - Abdominal pain
  - Jaundice
  - Weight loss
  - Abdominal mass
  - Nausea, vomiting
  - Back pain
  - Pancreatitis
- Symptomatic nonfunctional PNETs are **larger** than incidental ones (**2.5 vs. 1.8 cm**) and **more likely to have involved nodes** at diagnosis

## Nonfunctional Tumors — Incidental Discovery

- Approximately **35% of PNETs are discovered incidentally**
- Frequency is **increasing** as use of high-quality axial imaging increases

## Nonfunctional Tumors — Outcomes of Incidental PNETs

- In one series of incidentally discovered PNETs:
  - **19%** benign histopathologic findings → **89% 5-year OS**
  - **52%** uncertain histology → **93% 5-year OS**
  - **28%** malignant pathologic features → **50% 5-year OS**

## Nonfunctional Tumors — Biomarker Caveats

- Blood biomarkers that can be elevated with PNETs:
  - Chromogranin A, pancreastatin, pancreatic polypeptide, neuron-specific enolase, tachykinins
- **Limitations:**
  - Lack of laboratory standards
  - Varying sensitivity and specificity
  - Serum chromogranin A can be elevated in kidney/heart disease, proton-pump inhibitor use, and other non-NEN tumors
- **Currently, no data justify using these biomarkers in isolation** for diagnosis or treatment decision making

## Imaging — Goals & Modalities

- Imaging and endoscopy are used for:
  - Primary tumor detection
  - Staging
  - Surgical planning
  - Evaluation of **somatostatin receptor (SSTR)** expression
- Modalities used most often:
  - **CT**, **MRI**, **endoscopic US (EUS)**, standard **US**
  - **Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS)**
  - **Positron-emission tomography (PET)**

## Imaging — CT: The First Stop

- CT is often the **first modality** used to image PNETs
- Valuable for detection of **primary, regional, and metastatic disease**
- More sensitive for **hepatic metastases** than for primary tumors

## FIGURE 65.2 — CT Appearance of a PNET

> **FIGURE 65.2** — Arterial phase of a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showing an **early enhancing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor** in the **head and uncinate process** of the pancreas (**white arrow**), with a **necrotic node medially** (**red arrow**).

**Teaching points:**

- PNETs and their metastases are **hypervascular** → best seen in the **arterial phase**
- Lesions **wash out** in the venous and delayed phases

## CT — Sensitivity

- Sensitivity for tumors **> 2 cm: 80% to 100%**
- Can detect some PNETs **smaller than 0.5 cm**
- However, more likely to **miss small lesions** compared with EUS

## CT — Contrast Protocol Matters

- CT should be obtained with **oral and IV contrast**
- **IV contrast:** essential — PNETs and metastases are hypervascular, best seen in **arterial phase** (washout in venous/delayed phases)
- **Oral contrast:** helpful for visualizing the **duodenum**

## MRI — When to Use

- Considered a **second-line test** for primary PNET detection
- Indications:
  - Superior delineation of **hepatic metastases** required
  - **Iodinated contrast allergy**
  - **Renal failure**
- Should also be obtained **with IV contrast**

## MRI — Tumor Characteristics

- PNETs are:
  - **Hypointense on T1**
  - **Hyperintense on T2**
- As with CT, lesions **< 1 cm may be missed**, regardless of contrast administration

## Ultrasound — EUS

- US is most commonly:
  - **Combined with endoscopy (EUS)**, or
  - Used **intraoperatively** for tumor localization
- EUS may be used to identify:
  - The **primary tumor**
  - **Local nodal involvement**
  - With **fine needle biopsy** → tissue diagnosis

## Ultrasound — Performance

- **EUS with FNB:** diagnostic accuracy of **90%**
- **EUS sensitivity:** 79% to 82%; can detect tumors as small as **2 to 3 mm**
- **Intraoperative US** (e.g., for insulinomas): sensitivity **80% to 100%**
- Caveat: EUS and IOUS are **highly operator dependent**

## SSTR Imaging — The Rationale

- Imaging is **critical to clarify SSTR status** of the disease
- Scintigraphy with **radiolabeled SST analogs** is a useful tool in diagnosis and treatment determination
- There are **five somatostatin receptor subtypes (SSTR1–SSTR5)**
- **SSTR2** is frequently expressed on **well-differentiated NETs** and serves as the **primary receptor** for somatostatin analogue imaging **and treatment**

## OctreoScan and SPECT

- Original somatostatin analogue imaging: the **OctreoScan**, using radiotracer **indium-111–DPTA-octreotide**
- Basic form: whole-body planar image — dark spots indicate radiotracer bound to **SSTR2** (and to a lesser extent SSTR5 and SSTR3)
- Most centers add **SPECT** (single-photon emission CT): axial 3D imaging + functional scintigraphic image
- In one study, adding **SPECT improved lesion detection by 52%**

## 68Ga-PET/CT — Ligands

- Most modern SSTR-based imaging: **PET combined with CT**, using **gallium-68**–labeled somatostatin analogues:
  - **68Ga-DOTA-Tyr(3)-octreotide (DOTATOC)**
  - **68Ga-DOTA-1-Nal(3)-octreotide (DOTANOC)**
  - **68Ga-DOTA-Tyr(3)-octreotate (DOTATATE)**
- Each ligand varies in SSTR subtype affinity, but these differences are **not clinically significant**

## 68Ga-PET/CT — Performance & Approval

- **68Ga-PET/CT is the preferred functional imaging** of choice over OctreoScan
- Detects both **functional and nonfunctional PNETs**
- Studies consistently demonstrate **superiority over conventional imaging** (CT, MRI, OctreoScan) for detection of NET primary tumors and metastases
- Approved for **general use in the United States in 2016**

## 68Ga-PET/CT — Pitfalls

- Care must be taken to differentiate NETs from **physiologic uptake of 68Ga**, seen in:
  - **Uncinate process** of the pancreas
  - **Pituitary**
  - **Spleen** (or accessory spleen)
  - **Kidneys**

## 18FDG PET — Role in High-Grade Disease

- **18-Fluoro-deoxy-glucose PET** is most often used when the tumor is **high grade**
- Patients with PNETs **avid on 18FDG PET** are more likely to have **early disease progression** than those who are 18FDG PET negative

## Surgery — Goals of Resection

- Cure requires excision of:
  - The **primary PNET**
  - **Regional nodal disease**
  - **Distant metastases**
- Cure is **unlikely in the setting of distant metastases**
- Despite this, patients may still **derive benefit** from surgical resection in metastatic disease → evaluate with a surgeon familiar with **NET-directed operations**

## Surgery — Indications for Resection

In general, resection is indicated for:

1. **Functional, symptomatic PNETs**
2. **Isolated G1 or G2 PNETs > 2 cm**
3. **Metastatic disease** in which **all visible metastases can be resected**

## Surgery — Palliative Resection

- **Palliative resection of the primary** and **hepatic debulking** may be considered when:
  - Symptomatic, advanced disease
  - The **liver is the only focus** of distant metastases
- Whether this affects overall survival is **unknown**

## The Small PNET Dilemma

- Generally accepted: **nonfunctional PNETs > 2 cm should be resected** (metastatic potential)
- **Much debate** exists about **smaller PNETs**
- In many centers: small tumors are **observed with serial imaging**, resected **if progression**
- Evidence for this approach is **conflicting** — see the next three studies

## Small PNETs — Lee et al. (2012)

- Compared nonfunctional PNETs **< 4 cm**:
  - **Nonoperative:** n = 77; median tumor size **1 cm**
  - **Resection:** n = 56; median tumor size **1.8 cm**
- In the operative group: **9% had positive nodes** (median tumor size 2.4 cm)
- Mean follow-up: **3.75 years** (maximum, 12.75 years)

## Small PNETs — Lee et al.: Results

- In the **nonoperative** group:
  - Median primary tumor size **did not change** during follow-up
  - **No disease progression**
  - **No disease-specific mortality**
- Conclusion: **small PNETs can be safely managed nonoperatively**

## Small PNETs — Sadot et al.

- Reviewed **464 incidentally discovered, sporadic, small (< 3 cm), stage I–II PNETs**
- **104 were recommended for observation**

## Small PNETs — Sadot et al.: Results

- **Observation group:** at last follow-up:
  - Median tumor size unchanged (**1.2 cm**, P = .7)
  - **No patient developed metastases**
- **Resection group:**
  - Low-grade pathology in **72 (95%)** tumors
  - **5 (6%) developed recurrence** — after a median of **5.1 years** (range, 2.9–8.1)
- **No patient in either group died from disease**; death from other causes in 11 of 181 (6%)
- Conclusion: **observation of stable, small, incidental PNETs is reasonable** in selected patients

## Small PNETs — The NCDB Counterpoint

- NCDB study of **localized, nonfunctioning PNETs < 2 cm** (n = 380):
  - **Resection → median OS > 5 years** vs. **2.3 years** with observation
- **Important caveat:** NCDB inclusion requires a **tissue diagnosis** → many incidentally found, imaging-followed tumors were **not included**

## Small PNETs — Bottom Line

- Optimal management of nonfunctional tumors **< 2 cm is unclear**
- In patients with **significant comorbidities**, observation seems reasonable
- Reminder: **pancreas-directed operations are not without risk**

## Surgery — Perioperative Morbidity

- In the Lee et al. (2012) series:
  - **46%** of surgically treated patients had a **perioperative complication**
  - Most common: **pancreatic fistula**

## FIGURE 65.3 — Distal Pancreatectomy

> **FIGURE 65.3** — **A,** Intraoperative view of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor located in the **body of the pancreas**. **B,** Specimen resulting from **distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy**.

## Distal Pancreatectomy — Technical Points

- **Body and tail lesions** → **distal pancreatectomy**
- Larger tumors commonly **invade the splenic vein** → **splenectomy** often performed
- If tumors are small and do **not** invade the vein → **splenic preservation** should be considered

## Surgery by Location — Head Lesions

- Tumors in the **head**, especially if large → **pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD)**
- **Small tumors in the head** can be considered for **enucleation**

## Enucleation — Concept

- More limited procedures (e.g., enucleation) are acceptable for **small, isolated PNETs**
- In well-selected patients: associated with **relatively low complication rates**
- Generally performed for:
  - **Insulinomas**
  - Small, isolated **gastrinomas** or **nonfunctional PNETs**

## FIGURE 65.4 — Enucleation

> **FIGURE 65.4** — **A,** Enucleation of an **insulinoma in the uncinate process**; tumor circled, duodenum laterally (D), superior mesenteric vein pulled medially for exposure (arrow). **B,** Enucleation of a PNET at the **superior aspect of the neck of the pancreas**; tumor (circle) mostly detached and rolled inferiorly over the pancreas. GDA, gastroduodenal artery; PV, portal vein; SV, splenic vein.

## Enucleation — Comparative Outcomes

- Three recent studies of enucleation for **small (1–3 cm) PNETs**
- Compared with **PD or distal pancreatectomy**, enucleation showed:
  - **Less blood loss**
  - **Shorter operative times**
  - **Fewer postoperative complications**
  - **Less pancreatic insufficiency**
- Can be approached safely via **laparotomy or laparoscopy**
- Should be **reserved for PNETs most likely to be benign**

## Enucleation — Selection Criteria & Technique

- From a technical standpoint, enucleation should only be considered for PNETs that are:
  - **2 to 3 mm away from the main pancreatic duct**
  - **< 2 cm** in size
  - Located relatively **near the surface** of the pancreatic parenchyma
- **Intraoperative US** should be used to visualize the pancreatic duct during the procedure

## Minimally Invasive Distal Pancreatectomy

- To improve recovery, distal pancreatectomy may be performed **laparoscopically or robotically**
- **Meta-analysis:** 18 studies, **1814 patients** with tumors amenable to distal pancreatectomy
  - **43%** laparoscopic resection; remainder laparotomy

## Laparoscopic DP — Meta-analysis Findings

- Laparoscopic group had:
  - **Shorter length of stay**
  - **Less blood loss**
  - **Fewer postoperative complications**
- Encouragingly, **no difference** in:
  - Margin positivity
  - Postoperative pancreatic fistula
  - Mortality
- Caveat: **trend toward fewer lymph nodes sampled** with the laparoscopic approach

## Resecting the Primary in Advanced Disease — The Debate

- **Argument against resection:** unlikely to obtain a curative (R0) resection → risk of a large operation without survival benefit
- **Counter-evidence:** Hill et al. (2009) — see next slide

## FIGURE 65.5 — Hill et al. Survival Analysis

> **FIGURE 65.5** — In a retrospective SEER analysis, Hill and colleagues demonstrated that OS of PNET patients can be **improved if surgical resection of the primary can be performed**. Patients in whom surgery was recommended but not performed (including palliative procedures) had median survival **on par with patients in whom surgery was not offered** — across **all disease stages**. *(Modified from Hill JS, et al. Cancer 2009;115:741–751.)*

| Group | n |
|---|---|
| Resection performed | 310 |
| Recommended, but not resected | 53 |
| Surgery not recommended | 302 |

*Log-rank P < .0001*

## Hill et al. — Results & Interpretation

- Patients who had surgery: median OS **114 months** vs. **35 months** with medical management
- The trend **persisted even in the M1 subgroup** — surgery conferred a significant survival advantage
- **Caution:** significant **selection bias** in such studies — benefit of resection cannot be assumed
- Practical approach:
  - Primary **growing** and/or at risk of complications (e.g., bleeding) → **consider removing the primary**
  - Small, **asymptomatic, stable** primary in metastatic disease → **watch**

## MEN1 — Surgical Complexity

- Resection of the primary in **MEN1** is **more difficult and more controversial** than sporadic PNET:
  - **Partial pancreatectomy only treats the tumor identified at operation**
- Three PNET types most frequently encountered in MEN1:
  - **Insulinomas**
  - **Gastrinomas**
  - **Nonfunctional tumors**
- Imaging frequently shows **multiple small tumors**; functional and nonfunctional PNETs often **coexist**
- **Resection of functional tumors is generally recommended**

## MEN1 — Insulinomas

- Insulinomas in MEN1 typically arise in the **tail of the pancreas**
- When **many PNETs** are seen at surgery:
  - **Distal pancreatectomy** (to the level of the superior mesenteric vein) has been suggested
- PNETs in the **head** should be **enucleated**, if possible
- **Cure rates of 90%** achieved with this method

## MEN1 — Gastrinomas

- More difficult to treat than insulinomas:
  - **Biochemical cure is rare**
  - **Recurrence is frequent**
- In MEN1, gastrinomas tend to occur in the **duodenum**

## MEN1 — Duodenal Exploration

- In addition to careful **US examination of the pancreas**:
  - **Transillumination of the duodenum**
  - **Duodenotomy** for palpation of the wall
- Purpose: ensure **excision of all gastrinomas**

## MEN1 — Escalating to Extensive Surgery

- If duodenal gastrinomas **preclude simple excision**:
  - Consider **pancreas-preserving total duodenectomy** + enucleation of as many PNETs **> 1 cm** as possible
- **More extensive surgery** for primary gastrinomas **> 2 cm**:
  - More likely to see **resolution of ZES**
  - Lower risk of **hepatic metastases** vs. unresected similarly sized PNETs
- Gastrinoma primary in the **head**, especially **> 2 cm** → **PD is indicated**

## VHL — Surgical Considerations

- PNETs are found in **12% to 17% of patients with VHL**
- Approximately **17%** of those tumors will eventually **metastasize**

## VHL — Libutti Criteria & Validation

- **Libutti et al. (1998):** PNETs **> 3 cm should be resected**
  - Median size of PNETs in metastatic disease: **5 cm** vs. only **2 cm** in localized disease
- **Prospective validation:** 44 VHL patients with PNETs observed or resected **based on size**
  - Median follow-up **32 months** (range, 4–110 months)
  - **None** who underwent resection developed metastatic disease

## VHL — Blansfield Additions

- **Blansfield et al. (2007)** suggested additional risk features:
  - **Germline mutation in exon 3**
  - **Doubling time < 500 days**
- These features correlate with PNETs likely to metastasize
- Libutti (2000) confirmed most VHL patients with metastatic PNETs have **exon 3 mutations**
- **No study has validated** the inclusion of the Blansfield guidelines along with size criteria

## Metastatic Disease — Nodal Involvement

- At least **20% of PNET patients** have spread to **regional lymph nodes** at diagnosis
- **No guideline** exists on the number of lymph nodes to sample, or a requirement for formal lymphadenectomy
- However: lymph node metastases are associated with **increased risk of recurrence**
- Recent studies suggest a **more aggressive approach may be of benefit**

## Lymphadenectomy — Bartsch et al. (2012)

- **48 cases of sporadic gastrinoma with N1 disease**
- Primary tumor resected (variety of procedures) + **systematic lymphadenectomy**:
  - Peripancreatic and pancreaticoduodenal nodes
  - Nodes in the hepatoduodenal ligament along the hepatic artery
  - Aortocaval nodes
- **Formal lymphadenectomy = > 10 lymph nodes** pathologically assessed

## Lymphadenectomy — Results & Supporting Evidence

- **Bartsch:** formal lymphadenectomy → significantly higher **postoperative biologic cure rate**:
  - Fasting gastrin **< 125 pg/mL** + negative secretin stimulation test
  - Trend toward improved **disease-free survival**
- In sporadic gastrinoma patients treated by **enucleation only vs. more extensive procedure + formal lymphadenectomy**:
  - Significant improvement in **time-to-recurrence** with lymphadenectomy

## Hepatic Metastases — The Problem

- Hepatic metastases are seen in approximately **50% of PNET patients**
- **Curative resection is rarely achieved**
- However, surgical reduction of hepatic tumor burden may:
  - **Diminish symptoms** from functional tumor syndromes
  - **Delay liver failure** secondary to hepatic replacement

## Hepatic Metastases — Cytoreductive Surgery

- Surgical debulking is appropriate when an estimated **90% reduction of metastatic burden** can be achieved
- **Tumor grade should be considered** — debulking reserved for **lower-grade tumors**
- **Gold-standard cytoreductive technique: formal segmental resection**

## Ablation & Embolization

- Additional valuable techniques (advantages: preserve maximal normal liver parenchyma, lower complication rates):
  - **Wedge resection**
  - **Enucleation**
  - **Ablation** (radiofrequency or microwave)
  - **Hepatic artery embolization**
- Ablative techniques are **best for small-volume isolated metastases (< 5 cm)**
- Because most patients have **large, multiple tumors** → **hepatic artery embolic therapy** is often the most rational and preferred approach
- A **standard set of criteria** guides patient selection

## Transplantation

- Preoperative factors predicting **poor outcome**:
  - Primary located in the **pancreas or duodenum**
  - Need for **upper abdominal exenteration**
  - **Hepatomegaly**
- A patient presenting for transplant with a **PNET and hepatomegaly**: estimated 5-year survival **12%**
- Improves to **68%** if the patient has only **one or neither** of those factors
- **Transplant is rarely curative**

## Nonsurgical Management — Indications

Medical management is indicated for patients with:

- **Clinical symptoms** (hormone secretion and/or tumor bulk)
- **High tumor burden**
- **Metastatic disease**
- **High-grade disease** (particularly nonlocalized)
- **Progressive disease**

## Medical Management — Goals

- In the presence of metastases, treatment is **almost always noncurative**
- Goals should be to:
  - **Improve quality of life**
  - **Extend survival**

## Medical Therapy — Insulinomas (Diazoxide)

- Hypoglycemia of insulinomas can be treated with **diazoxide (200–600 mg/day)**
- **Fast-acting drug**, but may work in only **~50% of patients**
- Nearly **50% experience side effects**:
  - Fluid retention
  - Nausea
  - Hirsutism
  - Palpitations
  - Anorexia

## Medical Therapy — ZES (PPIs)

- Symptoms of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome are best treated with **proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs)**
- Dose should be **titrated to effect**
- Non-surgical candidates can be sustained on PPIs **long term**:
  - Patients treated **> 10 years do not develop tachyphylaxis**
  - May develop **achlorhydria** → can lead to **nutritional deficiencies**

## Systemic Therapy — Choosing a Strategy

- Given PNET heterogeneity, systemic therapy strategy depends on:
  - **Tumor functional status**
  - **Pathologic grade**
  - **SSTR avidity** on functional imaging
  - **Disease bulk**
  - **Disease behavior**

## Somatostatin Analogs — Mechanism & Role

- Most well-differentiated NETs **express SSTRs** (most commonly **subtype 2**) and are avid on functional imaging (OctreoScan or 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT)
- **SSAs (octreotide, lanreotide):**
  - Typically **first-line** for advanced, progressive, **SSTR-avid PNETs**
  - Also moderate **symptoms** in functional PNETs
- **Antiproliferative mechanism:** bind primarily **SSTR2, SSTR5, SSTR3** → stimulate **cell-cycle arrest** and **inhibition of mitosis**

## Somatostatin Analogs — Tolerability

- Well-tolerated class; most common side effects:
  - Flatulence
  - Diarrhea or steatorrhea
  - Nausea
  - Cholelithiasis
  - Glucose intolerance

## PROMID Study — Octreotide

- **85 patients** with well-differentiated, functioning and nonfunctioning, **metastatic midgut NETs**
- Randomized: **42 octreotide LAR** vs. **43 placebo** (intramuscularly monthly)
- Primary endpoint: **progression-free survival (PFS)**

## PROMID — Results

- At 6 months, stable disease:
  - **Octreotide: 66.7%**
  - **Placebo: 37.2%**
- Median time to tumor progression:
  - **Octreotide: 14.3 months**
  - **Placebo: 6 months** (P < .001)

## CLARINET Study — Lanreotide

- **204 patients** with advanced, well- or moderately differentiated, **nonfunctioning**, low- or intermediate-grade NETs
- Randomized: **101 lanreotide** vs. **103 placebo** (monthly)
- At 24 months, estimated progression-free:
  - **Lanreotide: 65.1%**
  - **Placebo: 33%**
- Median PFS: **not reached vs. 18 months** (P < .001)

## SSAs — NCCN Recommendations

- PROMID and CLARINET illustrated the **clinically relevant antiproliferative effects** of SSAs in patients with NETs
- **NCCN guidelines** recommend **octreotide LAR or lanreotide first-line**:
  - For **relief of symptoms** (in the setting of hormone release)
  - For **tumor control** in patients with **SSTR-avid NETs**

## Targeted Therapies — Overview

- **Sunitinib** and **everolimus** have both demonstrated activity and are **approved** for advanced PNETs
- Because of the **highly vascular nature** of PNETs, **inhibition of angiogenesis** is a favorable target
  - **Sunitinib:** multitargeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor — blocks **VEGF, PDGFR, and c-KIT**
  - **Everolimus:** **mTOR inhibitor**

## Everolimus — Mechanism

- The **mTOR pathway** regulates:
  - Cell survival
  - Proliferation
  - Metabolism
- Several genes in the pathway are important in the development of **familial syndromes (NF1, TS)**
- FDA approval for PNETs was established through **RADIANT-3**

## RADIANT-3 — Design

- **410 patients** with **advanced and progressive PNETs**
- Randomized:
  - **207 everolimus** vs. **203 placebo** daily, in conjunction with best supportive care

## RADIANT-3 — Results

- Everolimus associated with improved median PFS by **6.4 months**:
  - **11 months vs. 4.6 months**
- Increased response rate: **5% vs. 2%**
- Well tolerated; most adverse events were **grade 1 or 2**:
  - Stomatitis, rash, diarrhea, fatigue, upper respiratory infections

## Everolimus — Overall Survival

- Later survival analysis:
  - Everolimus arm: median OS **44 months** — the **longest OS reported in a phase III study** for this population
- **Crossover** from placebo to open-label everolimus was allowed at progression:
  - **172 patients (85%)** of the placebo group crossed over
  - Placebo cohort OS: **37.7 months**

## Everolimus — A Bonus in Insulinomas

- Everolimus can be **effective in treating insulinomas**
- One of its known side effects is **induction of glucose intolerance** — which may **eliminate the symptoms of hypoglycemia** in some patients

## Everolimus + Octreotide — Phase II

- Phase II study of the **synergistic effects** of everolimus and octreotide:
  - 50 NET patients, **14 with PNETs**
- In the PNETs:
  - **14% partial response**
  - **None had complete response**
- Despite relatively poor response rates: **clinical benefit rate was 92%** — better than many other drug combinations

## Sunitinib — Mechanism

- **Sunitinib is an effective therapy for PNETs**
- Multitargeted **receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor**:
  - Blocks **VEGF**
  - Blocks **PDGFR**
  - Blocks **c-KIT**

## Sunitinib — Phase III Trial

- Randomized, multinational, phase III study:
  - **171 patients** with advanced, well-differentiated PNETs
  - Best supportive care + **daily sunitinib** vs. **placebo**
- Study was **stopped early** because:
  - Serious adverse events and deaths observed in the **placebo group**
  - PFS **favored sunitinib**

## Sunitinib — Phase III Results

- Median PFS:
  - **Sunitinib: 11.4 months**
  - **Placebo: 5.5 months**
- A notable difference in **objective overall response** was also seen (9.3% in the sunitinib arm)

## Key Takeaways — Classification & Diagnosis

- PNETs are the **second most common pancreatic tumor**; incidence is rising
- **WHO 2017 grading** (Ki-67/mitotic count) is the most significant prognostic tool
- All PNETs have malignant potential — but behavior is heterogeneous
- ~30% are functional (insulinoma, gastrinoma, glucagonoma, VIPoma, somatostatinoma); functional tumors are detected earlier and fare better
- **68Ga-PET/CT** is the preferred functional imaging modality; CT/MRI/EUS remain core tools

## Key Takeaways — Surgery

- Resect functional symptomatic tumors, isolated G1/G2 tumors > 2 cm, and resectable metastatic disease
- Small incidental nonfunctional PNETs can often be **observed** — evidence is conflicting; tailor to comorbidities
- **Enucleation** and **minimally invasive distal pancreatectomy** offer lower morbidity in selected patients
- Hepatic debulking (≥90% cytoreduction) can palliate and delay liver failure; transplant is rarely curative
- Familial syndromes (MEN1, VHL) demand specialized, individualized surgical strategies

## Key Takeaways — Medical & Systemic Therapy

- **Diazoxide** (insulinoma) and **PPIs** (ZES) control hormonal syndromes
- **SSAs (octreotide, lanreotide):** first-line for SSTR-avid advanced PNETs — antiproliferative benefit proven in PROMID and CLARINET
- **Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor):** PFS benefit in RADIANT-3; longest reported median OS (44 months); may ameliorate hypoglycemia in insulinomas
- **Sunitinib (TKI):** PFS benefit (11.4 vs. 5.5 months) in advanced well-differentiated PNETs
- Treatment selection depends on functional status, grade, SSTR avidity, bulk, and behavior

## Summary

- PNETs are rare but increasingly prevalent neuroendocrine neoplasms with distinct molecular underpinnings (MEN1/DAXX/ATRX, mTOR pathway)
- Prognosis is driven by **grade, stage, functional status, and age**
- Management is **multidisciplinary**: surgery, liver-directed therapy, and systemic treatments
- Despite often indolent behavior, metastatic PNETs are generally incurable — goals are **quality of life and survival extension**
- Familiarity with familial syndromes, imaging modalities, and the evolving systemic therapy landscape is essential for optimal patient care
